evaluation_inputs.system_description: An Event framework where the application logic and framework are highly inter-dependent. The Main module is part of the framework, and the Event Manager interacts directly with application handlers. It features an Event Queue and a base Handler component extended by standard and application-specific handlers.

phase_1_discovery.initial_documentation_status: Fully developed architecture with class diagrams, component descriptions, and defined component interactions.
evaluator_inquiry_questions: Can the components of the architecture be reused for future projects?
Can the framework be expanded in the future to accommodate a new application or new components?
Will the system handle any input given by the user and handle invalid input?
Is the architecture consistent in behavior?
Can any new application-specific functionality be added to the architecture?
Can the system be modified in short time and cost-effective manner?
Does the architecture perform its event-processing task properly?

hardware_view_description: System accepts input via Command Line Interface (CLI)
Single processor execution implied (sequential event processing)
runtime_constraints: Events must be dispatched in a First-Come-First-Served (FIFO) pattern
System must maintain an 'idle wait' state until input is received
Application logic is embedded within framework components

quantitative_model_parameters.performance_proxy: Number of components involved in a transaction
quantitative_model_parameters.transaction_speed: Qualitative (Slow due to high number of components involved)

questions: Does the system allow unauthorized access?
Does the architecture portray data confidentiality?
Does the architecture process any task in the fastest possible speed?

business_goals: Provide an Event framework to be used by an application
Handle and process events through component interaction
Allow application components to utilize the framework services

Must maintain system in idle state until input is received

children.scenario_description: An unauthorized user attempts to access the system through the CLI, and the system must prevent access.
The system maintains proper data encapsulation and secure data structures during event handling.
Under normal CLI input, the system processes operations at the fastest possible speed given the event-driven architecture.
Given queued events, the system dispatches them in first-come-first-served order while remaining responsive enough to perform exactly as required.
If a failure occurs during event processing, the system should recover immediately.
When the user provides invalid input via the CLI, the system handles the error without breaking event processing.
Across repeated event-processing cycles, the architecture exhibits consistent behavior.
The framework is complete, clear, and performs exactly as required.
New demands on system functionality can be accommodated in the framework.
The framework can be modified in a short time and in a cost-effective manner.
The system can change from a command-driven interface to a window-based interface.

architectural_approaches.approach_name: Event-driven architecture with FIFO event queue
architectural_approaches.description: The supplied architecture uses a single Event Queue and a single Event Manager that dispatches events in first-come-first-served order under a CLI-driven, sequential execution model.

addressed_attributes.rationale: The queue and sequential dispatch provide a simple event-processing path, although the supplied evidence also indicates the transaction speed is slow due to the number of components involved.
A FIFO queue and idle-wait state support predictable event handling, but the evidence does not establish fault recovery mechanisms.
Using one queue and one manager supports a consistent event-processing structure.

architectural_approaches.approach_name: Framework with embedded application logic and extensible handlers
architectural_approaches.description: The architecture includes a base Handler component extended by standard and application-specific handlers, and the application logic is embedded within framework components that interact directly with the Event Manager.

addressed_attributes.rationale: Extensible handlers can add application-specific behavior, but the close coupling between framework and application logic may make change more difficult.
A base handler and extension mechanism can support reuse of common behavior across applications, though the supplied evidence also says the framework and application logic are highly inter-dependent.
Direct interaction between the Event Manager and application handlers supports event processing and STOP handling.

scenario_reference.text: No unauthorized access to the system

analysis_records.stimulus: An unauthorized user attempts to access the system
analysis_records.response_measure: Unauthorized access is denied; no protected handler or event-processing capability is exposed to the unauthenticated user.
architectural_decisions: CLI input is the system entry point
Event Manager interacts directly with application handlers
No explicit security mechanism is described in the supplied evidence
analysis_records.reasoning: The inputs mention a CLI and event framework structure, but they do not describe authentication, authorization, or access control. Therefore the architecture cannot be credited with satisfying this scenario from the supplied evidence.

risks.description: Security controls are not evidenced in the supplied architecture description.
risks.rationale: The architecture evidence covers event dispatch and handler extension, but not authentication, authorization, or input sanitization. This leaves unauthorized access prevention unverified.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Presence or absence of authentication/authorization at the CLI entry point

scenario_reference.text: All operations are processed in fastest possible speed

analysis_records.stimulus: User input arrives at the CLI and must be processed
analysis_records.response_measure: Operations complete as quickly as possible given the architecture; the supplied proxy is the number of components involved in a transaction.
architectural_decisions: Sequential event processing on a single processor
High number of components involved in a transaction
analysis_records.reasoning: The evidence explicitly states that transaction speed is qualitative and slow due to the high number of components involved. The single queue and sequential processing simplify control flow but do not support a claim of fastest possible speed.

risks.description: Transaction speed is expected to be slow because many components participate in each transaction.
risks.rationale: The quantitative model parameter explicitly says transaction speed is slow due to the high number of components involved.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Number of components involved in a transaction
Event queue depth / number of dispatch steps

tradeoff_points.parameter: Single FIFO queue and sequential dispatch

scenario_reference.text: Any failure should be followed by immediate recovery

analysis_records.environment: During event handling or handler execution
analysis_records.stimulus: A failure occurs in event processing
analysis_records.response_measure: The system recovers immediately and continues processing without significant interruption.
architectural_decisions: No recovery mechanism is described in the supplied evidence
analysis_records.reasoning: The architecture inputs do not describe retries, exception handling, failover, rollback, or checkpointing. Immediate recovery therefore remains unsupported by evidence.

risks.description: Immediate recovery capability is not evidenced.
risks.rationale: Without described recovery or fault-tolerance mechanisms, the architecture cannot be shown to recover immediately after failure.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Exception handling and recovery strategy in the Event Manager/handlers

scenario_reference.text: User errors in using system should be handled

analysis_records.response_measure: Invalid input is detected and handled without breaking the event-processing flow.
architectural_decisions: CLI input is accepted by the system
System must maintain an idle wait state until input is received
STOP handler is required for termination
analysis_records.reasoning: The idle-wait and CLI input constraints imply the system expects user input, but the evidence does not specify validation or error-handling behavior. The scenario is plausible but not demonstrated.

risks.description: Invalid input handling is not evidenced.
risks.rationale: The supplied inputs mention handling user input and idle wait, but do not describe validation, rejection, or recovery from malformed input.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Input validation logic at CLI boundary

scenario_reference.text: New demands on system functionality should be accommodated

analysis_records.stimulus: A new functional demand is introduced
analysis_records.response_measure: The framework is extended without major redesign and with acceptable effort.
architectural_decisions: Base Handler component is extended by standard and application-specific handlers
Application logic is embedded within framework components
Framework and application are highly inter-dependent
analysis_records.reasoning: The extensible handler structure supports adding new behavior, but embedding application logic inside framework components and the high inter-dependence reduce modifiability and increase change impact.

risks.description: Embedded application logic may increase the cost and effort of adding new functionality.
risks.rationale: High coupling between framework and application logic suggests changes may ripple through the framework.

non_risks.description: The base handler extension mechanism provides a path for adding new functionality.
non_risks.rationale: The evidence explicitly includes a base Handler component extended by standard and application-specific handlers.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Degree of coupling between framework components and application handlers

tradeoff_points.parameter: Embedding application logic in framework components

scenario_reference.text: Major parts of the framework should be re-usable for future architectures

analysis_records.stimulus: A future project needs to reuse the framework
analysis_records.response_measure: Major components can be reused with minimal adaptation.
architectural_decisions: Framework components are highly inter-dependent with application logic
Main module is part of the framework
analysis_records.reasoning: The base handler extension pattern supports reuse of common behavior, but the supplied evidence emphasizes inter-dependence between application logic and framework components, which reduces reuse across projects.

risks.description: High inter-dependence between framework and application logic may limit reuse.
risks.rationale: Components that depend on application-specific behavior are less portable to other projects.

non_risks.description: The base Handler abstraction supports partial reuse.
non_risks.rationale: Common handler behavior can be reused through extension even if the overall framework is tightly coupled.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Extent to which application-specific behavior is separated from framework behavior

scenario_reference.text: Framework modification is cost-effective, fast and in minimal time

analysis_records.stimulus: A change request requires framework modification
analysis_records.response_measure: The framework changes quickly and at low cost.
architectural_decisions: High inter-dependence between framework and application logic
analysis_records.reasoning: The architecture has an extension point, but the stated high coupling and component inter-dependence indicate changes are likely to propagate widely, increasing cost and time.

risks.description: Framework modifications may be slow and costly because of tight coupling.
risks.rationale: The inputs directly state that the application logic and framework are highly inter-dependent.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Coupling between framework and application logic

tradeoff_points.parameter: Single shared Event Manager and queue

scenario_reference.text: Components in framework interact in a coordinated manner

analysis_records.stimulus: Framework components process an event through the defined interactions
analysis_records.response_measure: Component interactions remain coordinated and consistent across event processing.
architectural_decisions: Base Handler extended by standard and application-specific handlers
analysis_records.reasoning: The architecture description explicitly states component interactions are defined and constrained through a single queue and event manager, which supports coordinated interaction. However, no behavioral conformance evidence is provided beyond the diagrammatic description.

non_risks.description: Defined component interactions support coordinated behavior.
non_risks.rationale: The architecture inputs explicitly state that component interactions are defined, and the event-processing flow is centralized.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Strictness of the component interaction contract

scenario_reference.text: Framework expansion is possible to allow for more sophisticated options

analysis_records.stimulus: A new component or more sophisticated option must be added
analysis_records.response_measure: The framework expands without major rework.
analysis_records.reasoning: Extension via handlers supports some expansion, but the coupling between framework and application logic suggests expansions may require changes across the framework.

risks.description: Expansion may require broad changes because extension is constrained by tight coupling.
risks.rationale: The evidence points to inter-dependent framework components, which can inhibit independent expansion.

non_risks.description: The handler extension model supports limited expansion.
non_risks.rationale: A base handler with standard and application-specific extensions provides a clear extension mechanism.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Amount of framework logic embedded in application-specific handlers

scenario_reference.text: Implementation allows for execution in different environments

analysis_records.stimulus: The framework is deployed in a different execution environment
analysis_records.response_measure: The system runs correctly without environment-specific redesign.
analysis_records.reasoning: The evidence is insufficient to establish portability. The CLI and sequential execution model do not by themselves demonstrate the ability to run in different environments.

risks.description: Portability is not supported by the supplied evidence.
risks.rationale: No abstraction or deployment-independence mechanism is described.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Environment-specific dependencies in the CLI/runtime stack

scenario_reference.text: Proper data encapsulation and secure data structures

analysis_records.stimulus: Framework components store and pass data between handlers
analysis_records.response_measure: Sensitive data remains encapsulated and protected from inappropriate access.
analysis_records.reasoning: Encapsulation is suggested by a handler-based design, but the supplied evidence does not explicitly describe secure data structures, access restrictions, or confidentiality mechanisms.

risks.description: Data confidentiality mechanisms are not evidenced.
risks.rationale: The architecture inputs do not describe encryption, access control, or secure storage.

non_risks.description: Handler abstraction may limit direct data exposure within event processing.
non_risks.rationale: A base handler abstraction can reduce direct coupling to internal data, but this is only an inference from the supplied structure.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Visibility and mutability of data shared between the Event Manager and handlers

scenario_reference.text: Overall consistent behavior expected from the architecture

analysis_records.stimulus: The system processes events repeatedly over time
analysis_records.response_measure: Behavior remains consistent across runs and inputs within the supported scope.
analysis_records.reasoning: A single manager and queue with FIFO dispatch promote deterministic behavior. This supports consistency, although it does not prove robustness under all failure conditions.

non_risks.description: A single FIFO event-processing path supports deterministic behavior.
non_risks.rationale: The runtime constraints explicitly require FIFO dispatch and a single queue, which reduce variation in event ordering.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Strict adherence to FIFO ordering and centralized dispatch

scenario_reference.text: Framework should be complete, clear and perform exactly as required

analysis_records.stimulus: The system is exercised according to its defined use cases
analysis_records.response_measure: The framework performs the required event-processing task completely and clearly.
architectural_decisions: Event Manager interacts directly with application handlers
analysis_records.reasoning: The architecture description supports core event-processing functionality and termination handling. However, completeness and clarity as required are subjective and not fully verifiable from the inputs.

risks.description: The exact completeness criteria are not defined in the supplied evidence.
risks.rationale: The scenario statement is broad and does not provide a measurable acceptance criterion.

non_risks.description: The architecture includes the main mechanisms needed for event processing and termination.
non_risks.rationale: The system description explicitly includes the Event Queue, Event Manager, and STOP handler.

scenario_reference.text: Hook up multiple applications to the framework at same time

analysis_records.stimulus: More than one application is connected to the framework
analysis_records.response_measure: Multiple applications can share the framework without interference.
architectural_decisions: High inter-dependence between framework and application logic
analysis_records.reasoning: The architecture evidence suggests a single shared event-processing path and direct framework/application coupling. That makes multi-application use possible only if handler isolation and multiplexing exist, but these are not described.

risks.description: A single shared event-processing path may not isolate multiple applications.
risks.rationale: The architecture specifies one Event Manager and one Event Queue but gives no evidence of per-application isolation.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Ability to separate application-specific state and routing within handlers

scenario_reference.text: Change interface from command-driven to window-based

analysis_records.stimulus: The interface is changed from CLI to a window-based interface
analysis_records.response_measure: The change is implemented without major redesign of framework internals.
architectural_decisions: CLI is the current input mechanism
Application logic is embedded within framework components
analysis_records.reasoning: Changing the input modality would likely require changes at the boundary between user input and event dispatch. Because application logic is embedded within framework components, the interface change may ripple into framework internals.

risks.description: A CLI-centric design may make UI replacement invasive.
risks.rationale: The current input mechanism is explicitly CLI-based, and the architecture does not describe a presentation abstraction.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Degree of separation between input interface and event-processing logic

tradeoff_points.parameter: Tight integration of UI/input and framework logic
